Hilal was eleven years old. He spoke slowly, and sometimes a word got stuck in his mouth, so he would repeat it once or twice until it came out.

Every night he climbed up to the roof of the house with his grandfather Abdullah. They sat on the straw mat and looked at the sky until they grew sleepy.

In the afternoons, the boys of the neighbourhood played in the square: Fahd, Bandar, and Adel. When Hilal came to talk to them, Fahd would repeat his words, stumbling just like him, and the others would laugh.

Then they called him "Father of the Stars," because he walked with his head up toward the sky.

Sometimes Hilal laughed along with them. Then he would go home and not say a word until dinner.

That night, when he climbed up to the roof, his grandfather pointed to a small, still star and said, "That is Al-Jadi, the North Star. All the stars move around, and it alone never leaves its place."

Then he said, "Our village is in its direction from the desert. Anyone who is lost at night and sees it will know his way."

Hilal repeated it slowly until he had learned it by heart.

The rain came at the end of winter, and Fahd said, "Tomorrow let's go out into the desert to gather desert truffles."

Hilal said, "I'll come with you." Fahd laughed and said, "You walk slowly and you talk slowly — when will we ever get back?"

When Grandfather Abdullah heard about it, he told them, "Take him with you. He won't slow you down." So they took him, though they did not want to.

They set out after noon and walked among the sand dunes, digging wherever the ground was cracked. They found lots of truffles — a kind of food like little potatoes that hides under the sand after the rain. They filled their bags and were very happy.

When the sun began to sink, Hilal said slowly, "The sun… is setting. Let's go back."

Fahd copied him as usual, they laughed, and they went on digging.

Then the sun set the way it sets in the desert, and a wind blew and wiped their footprints off the sand.

They stood among dunes that all looked the same. Bandar said, "We came from here." Adel said, "No, from over there." Fahd did not know anything, so he kept quiet.

The boys became very, very scared.

Hilal had lifted his head to the sky, as he did every night. He searched until he found the small, still star.

He said slowly, "That's… Al-Jadi. Our village… is that way."

The boys looked at one another. Then Fahd said in a quiet voice, "Walk in front of us, Hilal."

So Hilal walked in front, and they walked behind him in a line, none of them saying a word.

The words stumbled in his mouth, but his feet did not stumble on the way. Every time they climbed a dune, he lifted his head to the star and then went on.

After a long time in the night, the lights of the village appeared.

Their families had come out with lanterns to the edge of the village, and Grandfather Abdullah was among them.

The boys ran to them, and before his father could ask him anything, Fahd said, "Hilal is the one who brought us back."

Hilal said nothing. He put his bag of truffles in front of his grandfather.

The next night, four boys climbed up to Grandfather Abdullah's roof, not just one. They sat on the mat and looked at the sky.

Hilal showed them the stars, speaking slowly, and no one copied him.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ عَسَىٰ أَن يَكُونُوا خَيْرًا مِّنْهُمْ﴾

📖 Al-Hujurat 11. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
